newsitem.title: USA: Fight over US bank revenue bond powers to continue.
newsitem.headline: Fight over US bank revenue bond powers to continue.

text.p: U.S. banks won a skirmish on Wednesday in their effort to gain authority to underwrite municipal revenue bonds, but a leading opponent of the proposal predicted another battle lies ahead.

The House Banking Committee is debating amendments to legislation that would overhaul ageing U.S. banking laws. The proposal would give banks a host of new powers, including the ability to underwrite revenue bonds directly without having to establish a separate securities subsidiary.
Rep. Ken Bentsen, Democrat of Texas, tried and failed on Wednesday to strip the revenue bond provision from the bill.
Under Bentsen's amendment, defeated on a voice vote, revenue bonds would have remained "ineligible securities" for banks.
But despite the setback, Bentsen predicted the revenue provision would be deleted later in the legislative process.
If the banking committee ultimately approves the bill, which could happen as early as Thursday, the legislation then goes to the Commerce Committee for further consideration.
"I think it's possible the Commerce Committee will kick out muni revenue bonds," Bentsen told reporters, adding that in previous years the Commerce Committee had done so.
"It would not surprise me if they did something like that," he said.
Bentsen argued that revenue bonds were inherently riskier than general obligation bonds, which are bank eligible securities under current law.
Allowing banks to underwrite revenue bonds without requiring a separate subsidiary could give the banks an unfair advantage when competing with muni firms that are required to register, he said.
The revenue bond provision is opposed by the Securities Industry Association for that reason.

But proponents of the bond provision said the change would lower costs for municipal issuers by allowing small banks that cannot afford a securities subsidiary to get into the business, thus enhancing competition.
A former banker himself, Bentsen rejected that argument. "There's more than adequate competition," he said. "When I was a banker, I was never lonely competing for that business."
